heading: Strengthening HBCUs through Federal agency plans

tree.heading: Designating applicable agencies
tree.text: The Secretary, in consultation with the Executive Director, shall—

children.text: identify each Federal agency with which an HBCU—
has entered into a grant, contract, or cooperative agreement; or
is eligible to participate in the programs and initiatives under the jurisdiction of such Federal agency; and
designate each Federal agency so identified as an applicable agency.

tree.heading: Submitting agency plans
tree.text: Not later than February 1 of each year, the head of each applicable agency shall submit to the Secretary, the Executive Director, the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions of the Senate, the Committee on Education and Labor of the House of Representatives, and the President’s Board of Advisors an annual Agency Plan describing efforts to strengthen the capacity of HBCUs to participate or be eligible to participate in the programs and initiatives under the jurisdiction of such applicable agency as described in subsection (a)(1)(B).

tree.heading: Further requirements for submission and accessibility
tree.text: The Executive Director shall make all annual Agency Plan submissions publicly available online in a user-friendly format.

tree.heading: Agency plan content
tree.text: Where appropriate, each Agency Plan shall include—

children.text: a description of how the applicable agency intends to increase the capacity of HBCUs to compete effectively for grants, contracts, or cooperative agreements;
an identification of Federal programs and initiatives under the jurisdiction of the applicable agency in which HBCUs are underrepresented;
an outline of proposed efforts to improve HBCUs’ participation in such programs and initiatives;
a description of any progress made towards advancing or achieving goals and efforts from previous Agency Plans submitted under this section by such applicable agency;

a description of how the applicable agency plans to encourage public-sector, private-sector, and community involvement to improve the capacity of HBCUs to compete effectively for grants, contracts, or cooperative agreements, and to participate in programs and initiatives under the jurisdiction of such agency;
an identification of programs and initiatives not listed in a previous Agency Plan in which an HBCU may participate;
any other information the applicable agency determines is relevant to promoting opportunities to fund, partner, contract, or otherwise interact with HBCUs; and
any additional criteria established by the Secretary or the White House Initiative.

tree.heading: Agency engagement
tree.text: To help fulfill the objectives of the Agency Plans, the head of each applicable agency—

children.text: shall provide, as appropriate, technical assistance and information to the Executive Director to enhance communication with HBCUs concerning the applicable agency’s—
programs and initiatives described in subsection (d)(2); and
the preparation of applications or proposals for grants, contracts, or cooperative agreements; and
shall appoint a senior official to report directly to the agency head on the applicable agency’s progress under this section.

notes.heading: Codification
notes.text: This section was enacted as part of the HBCU Propelling Agency Relationships Towards a New Era of Results for Students Act or the HBCU PARTNERS Act, and not as part of the Higher Education Act of 1965 which comprises this chapter.

notes.heading: Change of Name
notes.text: Committee on Education and Labor of House of Representatives changed to Committee on Education and the Workforce of House of Representatives by House Resolution No. 5, One Hundred Eighteenth Congress, Jan. 9, 2023.

notes.heading: Findings and Purposes
notes.text: Pub. L. 116–270, § 2, Dec. 31, 2020, 134 Stat. 3325, provided that: “(a) Findings.—Congress finds the following:“(1) As many colleges and universities across the country kept their doors closed to African American applicants, historically Black colleges and universities (referred to in this section as ‘HBCUs’) played a central role in ensuring that African Americans could attain an excellent education. “(2) Today, HBCUs continue to play a critical role in ensuring that African Americans, and those of all races, can access high-quality educational opportunities. “(3) HBCUs enroll nearly 300,000 students, an estimated 70 percent of whom come from low-income backgrounds and 80 percent of whom are African American. “(4) According to the National Association For Equal Opportunity In Higher Education (referred to in this section as ‘NAFEO’), HBCUs make up just 3 percent of American institutions of higher education but serve more than a fifth of African American college students. “(5) According to the Thurgood Marshall College Fund (referred to in this section as ‘TMCF’), approximately 9 percent of all African American college students attend HBCUs. “(6) A March 2017 report from the Educa
